prompt.context: The national zoo has hired you to decide whether they should buy a panda. The client is looking to increase their revenues and profits.
prompt.question: Should the National Zoo acquire a panda? Assess the investment case and make a recommendation.

clarifying_info.q: How many visitors does the zoo receive per year?
What are the current ticket prices?
What are the costs associated with acquiring a panda?
clarifying_info.a: Acquisition: $890,000; Transportation: $335,000; Enclosure: $1,475,000; Panda Consultant: $200,000; Annual maintenance: $300,000

clarifying_info.q: Is there any benchmark data on visitor impact from panda acquisitions?
clarifying_info.a: After buying a panda, the San Diego Zoo increased their visitor count by 12% and maintained that level

clarifying_info.q: What discount rate should I use?
What is the expected lifespan of the panda?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the panda will live approximately 100 years; you may use a perpetuity

exhibits.title: Math: Acquisition of 1 Panda
exhibits.shows: A calculation table showing ticket counts by visitor type (adults and children), the 12% visitor increase, incremental ticket revenue, initial investment components, and cash flow timeline for a single panda acquisition
exhibits.data: Base tickets: 300,000 adults + 300,000 children; +12% = 336,000 each; incremental: 36,000 each; adult revenue at $15, child at $10; initial investment total: $(2,700,000); annual maintenance: $(300,000); perpetuity-based NPV calculation at 20% discount rate

exhibits.title: Math: Acquisition of 2nd Panda (bought at same time as 1st)
exhibits.shows: A calculation table for the incremental effect of adding a second panda simultaneously, including a second panda's cost structure, additional visitor uplift, and probability-weighted value of a baby panda sale
exhibits.data: 2nd panda base tickets: 300,000 adults + 300,000 children (pre-panda1 uplift baseline); +10% incremental = 30,000 each; initial investment: $(2,700,000); annual maintenance: $(300,000); baby panda sale price: $890,000 at 90% probability; NPV calculations at 20% discount rate

exhibits.title: Math: Acquisition of 2nd Panda (bought after 1st)
exhibits.shows: A calculation table for the incremental effect of a second panda purchased after the first, using the already-elevated post-panda-1 visitor base, and a probability-weighted baby panda sale
exhibits.data: Post-panda1 ticket base: 336,000 adults + 336,000 children; +10% incremental = 33,600 each; initial investment: $(2,700,000); annual maintenance: $(300,000); baby panda sale: $890,000 at 90% probability; NPV calculations at 20% discount rate

framework: Treat the acquisition as a capital investment: calculate NPV of incremental revenues minus costs
Identify incremental revenues: apply benchmark visitor uplift (12% from San Diego precedent) to current ticket mix
Build the cost structure: separate one-time capital costs (acquisition, transport, enclosure) from recurring costs (annual maintenance); treat consultant fee as sunk cost
Use perpetuity formula for ongoing cash flows given 100-year lifespan assumption and 20% discount rate
Assess whether to buy 1 or 2 pandas: a second panda adds 10% further uplift and introduces baby panda optionality
Identify risks and non-ticket revenue levers as next steps

questions.prompt: Calculate the NPV of acquiring one panda. Is it a good investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate incremental visitors (12% of 600,000 = 72,000 new visitors, split 50/50 adults/children), multiply by ticket prices to get incremental revenue, then subtract annualized maintenance cost to get perpetual annual CF, discount at 20%, and subtract initial investment. Consultant fee ($200,000) is a sunk cost and should be excluded. NPV > 0 signals a positive investment.

math.answer: NPV (1 panda) = $300,000. Positive NPV; acquisition is worthwhile.

questions.prompt: If the zoo buys a second panda at the same time as the first, would that be a good investment? Also consider that there is a 90% chance the two pandas procreate and the zoo can sell the baby panda at market price ($890,000) next year.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize the 2nd panda drives an additional 10% visitor increase ON TOP of the original base (not on the panda-1-adjusted base, since both are bought simultaneously). They must also note the same capital cost applies. The baby panda generates an expected cash inflow in year 1, discounted at 20%. NPV of panda 2 alone is negative, but adding baby panda optionality makes total NPV positive.

math.setup: Scenario A (2nd panda bought same time as 1st): additional 10% uplift on original 600,000 base = 60,000 new visitors (30,000 adults, 30,000 children). Incremental revenue: (30,000 x $15) + (30,000 x $10) = $450,000 + $300,000 = $750,000. Net annual CF = $750,000 - $300,000 = $450,000. Initial investment = $2,700,000. NPV (panda 2 standalone) = -$2.7M + ($0.45M / 0.20). Baby panda: expected sale = $890,000 x 90% = $801,000; NPV (baby) = $801,000 / 1.20. Combined NPV = -$2.7M + ($0.45M/0.20) + ($0.801M/1.20).
math.answer: NPV (panda 2 + baby panda, simultaneous purchase) = $217,500. Positive; the baby panda option makes the second panda worthwhile.

questions.prompt: Alternative: what if the zoo buys the second panda after having already bought the first? Recalculate the NPV of the second panda (plus baby panda) in this scenario.
questions.guidance: When the 2nd panda is purchased after the 1st, the attendance base has already been lifted 12% to 672,000 (336,000 adults, 336,000 children). The additional 10% uplift now applies to this elevated base, generating higher incremental revenues and a breakeven standalone NPV. Adding the baby panda optionality creates a substantially positive combined NPV.

math.setup: Post-panda-1 ticket base: 336,000 adults, 336,000 children. Additional 10% = 33,600 adults + 33,600 children. Incremental revenue: (33,600 x $15) + (33,600 x $10) = $504,000 + $336,000 = $840,000. Net annual CF = $840,000 - $300,000 = $540,000. Initial investment = $2,700,000. NPV (panda 2 standalone) = -$2.7M + ($0.54M / 0.20). Baby panda same as before: NPV = $667,500.
math.answer: NPV (panda 2 + baby panda, sequential purchase) = $667,500. Sequential purchase yields a better outcome than simultaneous.

brainstorming.prompt: Beyond ticket sales, what other revenue sources could the zoo explore in connection with the panda acquisition?

categories.name: Ticket and Pricing Levers
ideas: Increase general admission prices (run price sensitivity analysis first)
Introduce a 2-part tariff: a separate premium charge to view the pandas
Bundle panda viewing into a premium ticket tier

categories.name: Membership and Loyalty
ideas: Launch or promote annual zoo memberships with panda access
Create a panda-specific membership or sponsorship program

categories.name: Merchandise and Licensing
ideas: Sell panda-themed merchandise (plush toys, apparel, souvenirs)
License the panda's image for branded products

categories.name: Rentals and Partnerships
ideas: Rent or loan the pandas to other zoos for a fee
Partner with corporate sponsors for panda exhibit naming rights

categories.name: Competitive Positioning
ideas: Benchmark against other entertainment options (theme parks, aquariums) to justify premium pricing
Assess whether a panda differentiates the zoo enough to capture market share from competitors

recommendation: The National Zoo should acquire one panda: NPV is positive at $300,000, indicating value creation even before non-ticket revenue is considered
Acquiring a second panda is also value-accretive when the baby panda optionality is included (NPV of $217,500 if simultaneous, $667,500 if sequential); sequential purchase is the superior approach
The zoo should pursue additional revenue levers (merchandise, premium panda viewing fee, memberships) to further improve returns and reduce dependence on the single visitor-count assumption
risks: Pandas may not procreate, eliminating the $667,500 baby panda upside
Life expectancy risk: perpetuity assumption drives significant PV; a shorter panda lifespan materially reduces NPV
Visitor uplift may fall short of the 12% San Diego benchmark (different market, demographics, or competitive set)
Competitive risk: other zoos could acquire pandas, diluting the novelty premium
Financing risk: $2.7M upfront capital requirement needs to be funded; zoo must assess its balance sheet and fundraising capacity
next_steps: Conduct price sensitivity analysis to test whether ticket prices can be raised in conjunction with panda launch
Explore non-ticket revenue streams: merchandise, panda-viewing surcharge, memberships, corporate sponsorships
Investigate financing options (donations, bonds, government grants) given nonprofit status
Assess the zoo's operational capacity to care for pandas and whether additional staff/expertise is required
Consider phased approach: buy panda 1 first, evaluate visitor lift, then decide on panda 2
